title: Short Stuff: Black Loyalists
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Black Loyalists, African Americans (mostly enslaved) who fought for Great Britain in the American Revolutionary War. Covers Lord Dunmore's proclamation and his Ethiopian Regiment, the 1779 British offer of freedom to those who defected, the post-war resettlement of roughly 40,000 Loyalists in Nova Scotia, the Shelburne Riot, Thomas Peters' petition to London, and the 1792 voyage of ships from Halifax to Sierra Leone. Ends with the present-day Black Nova Scotian descendants, including Jason Farmer of Birchtown.
topics: freedom for slaves who fought for Britain

segments.title: Opening banter and topic introduction
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode and the choice of Black Loyalists as a Black History Month topic, noting it is overlooked in American history.

segments.title: Slavery in the colonies and the British recruitment offer
segments.summary: Slavery existed throughout the colonies, including the North, and was concentrated in the South. Before the war, the British sought to recruit enslaved Americans. Lord Dunmore, the British royal governor of Virginia, issued an early emancipation proclamation during a local rebellion, promising freedom to those who fought against their owners.

segments.title: Ethiopian Regiment and the 1779 proclamation
segments.summary: Between roughly 800 and 2,000 enslaved people and indentured servants fled plantations to fight for the British in Dunmore's Ethiopian Regiment, whose uniforms bore the slogan Liberty to Slaves. Later, in 1779, a second British proclamation offered freedom to enslaved people who reached British-held territory, which hurt plantation economies.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a short break before returning to the story.

segments.title: Post-war resettlement in Nova Scotia and the Shelburne Riot
segments.summary: After the war, Guy Carleton ordered Black Loyalists, who had been promised freedom, to leave for Nova Scotia. About 40,000 Loyalists, Black and white, arrived there, straining resources. Tensions erupted in the Shelburne Riot after David George baptized a white woman; whites attacked the Shelburne settlement, which was largely Black, for months until troops from Halifax restored order.

segments.title: Petition, Sierra Leone voyage and Nova Scotian descendants
segments.summary: Thomas Peters went to London to petition the Crown for land, but was redirected to a sanctuary in Sierra Leone. Fifteen ships sailed from Halifax as the first voyage of the Back to Africa movement. Some stayed in Nova Scotia and founded Birchtown, named after Samuel Birch. About 20,000 Black Nova Scotians today trace ancestry to Black Loyalists, including Jason Farmer, a ninth-generation descendant of Jupiter Farmer.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up, encouraging listeners to learn more and send email.
